messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

As a school principal, John had always been in control. He ran his school with precision and care, earning the respect of his students, teachers, and staff. But that all changed two years ago when he was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness. The memory of lying in the hospital bed, surrounded by beeping machines and sterile smells, is one that John's mind struggles to revisit. When he tries to recall the details of those fateful days, his mind goes blank. He remembers feeling scared, alone, and helpless, but the specifics remain shrouded in a haze. Sometimes, the emotions come flooding back without warning – the fear, the anxiety, the sense of desperation – but they're not accompanied by any clear images or memories. It's as if his body is reliving the trauma, tensing up in the same way it did when he was lying in that hospital bed. The smell of antiseptic or hospitals can transport John back to those dark days instantly. He'll catch a whiff of it on someone's clothes or in a public place, and suddenly he's flooded with anxiety. Even the smell of alcohol, which used to be a social lubricant for him, now makes his stomach turn. He avoids bars, parties, and any situation where he might encounter these smells. John has become increasingly isolated, cutting off contact with friends and family who don't understand what he's going through. He feels like a shadow of his former self – unrecognizable even to himself. He can't rely on his own body, which once seemed so strong and resilient, but now feels fragile and unpredictable. Simple medical procedures, like check-ups or routine exams, fill him with dread. As a way of coping, John has started rehearsing conversations before they happen. He'll script out entire dialogues in his head, trying to anticipate every possible scenario and outcome. It's a futile attempt to regain control over a life that now feels precariously balanced on the edge of chaos. The consequences of John's avoidance behaviors have been devastating. His relationships with friends and family are strained, and he's struggling to connect with his students and staff at school. He feels like he's just going through the motions, unable to find meaning or purpose in a life that was once so rich and fulfilling. Despite his best efforts, John can't shake the feeling that he's living on borrowed time. He's constantly on the lookout for signs of illness, convinced that his body is waiting to betray him again at any moment. This hypervigilance has taken a toll on his mental health, leaving him exhausted and demoralized. It was only when John realized he couldn't keep going on like this – that he needed help to break free from the grip of his trauma – that he finally sought therapy. He's hoping to find a way to reconcile with his past, to learn to trust himself and his body again. But for now, he's stuck in this limbo, unable to move forward or go back, tormented by memories he can't quite recall and emotions that feel like they're suffocating him.
